candidates.title: Reconcile cumulative readings before raising a leak alert
candidates.proposal:
Use an accounting audit to separate actual water movement from late paperwork. On each of five mornings, the caretaker records the existing cumulative meter reading, actual observation date/time, and entry date separately. Preserve original entries and annotate corrections. Compare cumulative totals between verified observations; never treat a copied or late-entered reading as a fresh morning measurement. A catch-up increase belongs to the whole elapsed interval, not solely to the day it was entered.

Use the maintenance roster to annotate cleaning and other known common water use over those same intervals. Compare verified interval consumption with comparable earlier intervals in the paper log, if available. An increase that survives timestamp correction and does not track cleaning becomes a suspected continuous-loss alert. Inspect accessible common pipes for corroborating wet joints, active dripping, or recurring puddles. Confirm a real common-pipe leak through observed escaping water; an unexplained meter increase alone remains unresolved.

This needs only the existing log, roster, and caretaker time. It assumes readings are cumulative and their observation times can be established. Keep records at building level and do not shut off apartments. Daily totals cannot establish that water escaped specifically overnight, and changing resident demand can resemble leakage. Without historical comparisons or visible evidence, five mornings may support an investigation rather than a confirmed diagnosis.
candidates.experiment: Compare the corrected interpretation with simple subtraction of consecutive log rows. Check whether an apparent spike disappears when a late entry is assigned to its actual interval. For a surviving alert, require another verified interval plus inspection for active leakage. After maintenance repairs a confirmed fault, check the next available reading and the repair location. Roll back the alert if corrected timing or documented cleaning explains it; if excess persists after repair, reopen the diagnosis rather than declaring success.

candidates.title: Move shared cleaning across a morning reading boundary
candidates.proposal:
Use a reversible change in cleaning timing to test whether shared use causes the apparent overnight loss. From the roster, identify one routine, movable water-using cleaning task. Coordinate with its assigned worker to move that task from before the morning meter observation to immediately afterward on one suitable day, preserving the task and its approximate scope. Do not defer essential hygiene or alter apartment service.

Over five mornings, obtain the existing readings at a consistent observation time and record actual observation times separately from entry times. Establish a usual cleaning interval, an interval from which the task has been moved, and the following interval receiving the moved task. With five readings there are four measured intervals, so choose the timing before starting. Mark the actual cleaning time on the roster.

If the apparent excess moves into the receiving interval, cleaning is a plausible explanation. If an elevated amount persists in the interval without that cleaning task, investigate accessible common pipes and other rostered uses. Confirm a real leak only with direct evidence of escaping water or subsequent maintenance findings. Resident demand remains uncontrolled, so a single contrast cannot prove a concealed leak.

The mechanism is a small operational intervention rather than an assumed cleaning allowance. It requires a movable task, cooperation from the rostered worker, and sufficiently reliable meter resolution. It uses no new sensors, reveals no unit-level consumption, and requires no shutdowns. Daily readings still cannot isolate overnight consumption precisely.
candidates.experiment: Compare the shifted-task pattern with the simpler explanation that every high daily total indicates leakage. The cleaning explanation gains support only if consumption falls in the interval losing the task and rises in the receiving interval; inconsistent results leave the case unresolved. Inspect any suspected pipe fault on another morning to confirm active escape. Restore the normal cleaning schedule immediately after the trial and verify completion on the roster. Withdraw a leak alert explained by the timing shift; retain an unresolved alert if the contrast is inconclusive.

candidates.title: Find recurring fresh leakage on a fixed common-pipe inspection route
candidates.proposal:
Make physical evidence the primary detector. For five mornings, walk the same accessible common-pipe route before scheduled cleaning where possible: exposed joints, risers, basement distribution pipes, and visible connections serving shared facilities. On paper, sketch locations and record active drips, wet tracks, puddles, and whether wetness appears fresh or unchanged. Observe only safely accessible areas; do not open fittings, operate valves, or enter apartments.

Use the maintenance roster to distinguish cleaning splash from pipe leakage. At a wet location, trace the visible water path toward its source. An observed drip emerging from a pipe defect confirms a leak. A puddle alone does not: condensation, drainage, and cleaning remain possible. Revisit ambiguous locations before cleaning on a later morning. If cleaning has already occurred, mark that visit as confounded rather than counting it as confirmation.

Use the daily meter log as supporting evidence. Record observation and entry times separately, reconcile delayed entries, and compare only valid elapsed intervals. A small visible leak may be real even when resident demand masks its effect on the building total. Conversely, unexplained consumption without a visible source remains an unresolved possible concealed leak.

This requires only a repeatable route, paper notes, the roster, and caretaker observation. Confirmed defects go to the responsible maintenance worker for repair planning without interrupting occupied apartments. The approach can locate accessible leaks quickly, but cannot exclude concealed leaks or establish overnight timing unless the caretaker directly observes leakage during that period.
candidates.experiment: Compare the route's findings with a simple meter-spike alert. Check whether it identifies an actively leaking joint on a morning without an unusual total, or rejects a wet patch attributable to cleaning. Require direct source observation before classifying a location as confirmed. After repair, revisit the source and downstream wet area on the next available morning; residual dampness alone is not continuing leakage. Roll back an unsupported location-specific diagnosis if tracing identifies cleaning or condensation. If active escape persists, reopen the repair request; do not reverse a sound repair merely because building consumption remains high.

candidates.title: Check the balance between existing main and downstream meters
candidates.proposal:
Use a water balance to detect losses between meters. This route requires the existing paper log to contain a building inlet meter and a complete set of downstream meters covering apartment and shared supplies. Check that prerequisite first; a log containing only one meter cannot support this method.

For each of the four intervals between five morning readings, subtract the combined downstream consumption from inlet consumption. A persistent positive difference can reveal water escaping upstream of the downstream meters, even when changing resident demand makes the building total difficult to interpret. The caretaker keeps individual readings private and reports only the building-level difference and any common-pipe findings.

Before calculating, verify which supplies each meter covers using existing maintenance information and accessible pipe routes. Use actual observation times, preserve original entries, and assign delayed entries to their true intervals. Reject comparisons with materially mismatched reading times. Subtract shared cleaning consumption only where an existing meter measures it. If cleaning draws from an unmetered branch, mark affected intervals as confounded using the roster; do not invent a cleaning allowance.

Compare the residual with earlier valid balances if the log provides them, considering meter resolution and possible meter disagreement. Without that background, a positive residual is an investigation lead, not a confirmed leak. Inspect the implicated common distribution section for an identifiable source before requesting repair planning that preserves occupied-apartment service.

This requires arithmetic, existing coverage information, and caretaker time. It cannot detect leaks downstream of apartment meters through the balance, and daily readings cannot establish overnight timing. Unknown branches, storage tanks, or inaccurate meters can defeat the inference.
candidates.experiment: For one valid interval, compare a simple high-total alert with the meter balance: high inlet use accompanied by matching downstream use should not trigger an upstream-leak diagnosis. Recalculate any residual after correcting timestamps and accounting for metered cleaning; disappearance falsifies that diagnosis. Confirm leakage through observed escape or maintenance findings. After repair, check the source and next valid balance. Withdraw the alert if corrected records or shared use explains it; if the residual persists, reopen the investigation rather than undoing a verified repair.

candidates.title: Test an unused common-water branch by reversible isolation
candidates.proposal:
Use an existing common-area shutoff valve to test whether a particular branch contributes unexplained consumption. Closing the branch changes the hydraulic path: a leak supplied by that branch should stop consuming water while it is isolated.

This route requires a readily operated existing valve and an exposed, traceable branch serving only nonessential common facilities. The caretaker must establish that it supplies no apartments, fire equipment, essential facilities, or equipment requiring water. Select a branch with no legitimate use during the trial, checked against the maintenance roster and its accessible outlets. If its coverage or use is uncertain, this route is unsuitable.

Use five morning readings to create four intervals: open, closed, open, closed. Change valve position immediately after each relevant morning reading; restore its original position after the fifth reading. Record observation times, cumulative readings, valve positions, and actual cleaning or maintenance activity on paper. Preserve original entries and reconcile delayed entries before comparing consumption over the actual elapsed intervals. Conduct normal cleaning through its usual supply; if it requires the selected branch, do not run this trial.

Repeatedly lower consumption during isolation would implicate the branch, although changing resident demand could mimic the pattern. Inspect the implicated common pipes for the source. Treat the meter pattern as localization evidence; confirm a leak through observed escaping water or a maintenance finding before arranging repair that preserves apartment service.

The trial needs only an appropriate existing valve, the log, the roster, and caretaker time. It cannot detect leaks elsewhere or establish that leakage occurs specifically overnight. Its feasibility depends on finding a safely isolatable, genuinely unused common branch.
candidates.experiment: Compare the open–closed pattern with a simple high-daily-total alert. Branch attribution weakens if consumption stays elevated while closed, fails to rise after reopening, or follows documented cleaning instead. Repetition strengthens the lead but does not prove leakage. Roll back immediately if unexpected common-service effects occur; restore the original valve position after the trial and verify normal common-facility operation. After a confirmed repair, inspect the source and next available valid reading. Withdraw an attribution explained by corrected records or legitimate use; investigate persistent excess separately.
